meta.title: Who really said "The whole problem with the world is that fools are so certain, and wiser people so full of doubts"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bertrand Russell never wrote this wording. His real 1933 line: the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt. This version is a paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The whole problem with the world is that fools are so certain, and wiser people so full of doubts'?
meta.ogDescription: Russell had the thought — but not in these words. What he actually wrote in 1933, and how the internet rewrote it.

answer.label: Not Russell’s wording — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Russell’s, but these words are not. In his essay The Triumph of Stupidity (10 May 1933) he wrote: “The fundamental cause of the trouble is that in the modern world the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt.” No source has been found for the popular “fools and fanatics” rewrite in Russell’s works — Quote Investigator ↗ traces it no earlier than 2001 and calls its provenance uncertain. The still shorter form quoted here, which drops “and fanatics” entirely, is a further degradation documented nowhere at all.

source.heading: What Russell actually wrote

docMeta.dd: 10 May 1933, as “Stupidity Rules” in the Hearst press
Mortals and Others: American Essays, 1931–1935, vol. 2
No known source in Russell’s works

source.excerpt:
Brute force plays a much larger part in the government of the world than it did before 1914, and what is especially alarming, force tends increasingly to fall into the hands of those who are enemies of civilisation. The danger is profound and terrible; it cannot be waved aside with easy optimism.

The fundamental cause of the trouble is that in the modern world the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt. Even those of the intelligent who believe that they have a nostrum are too individualistic to combine with other intelligent men from whom they differ on minor points. This was not always the case. A hundred years ago the philosophical radicals formed a school of intelligent men who were just as sure of themselves as the Hitlerites are; the result was that they dominated politics and that the world advanced rapidly both in intelligence and in material well-being.
trail: The real line, 1933. Russell’s essay The Triumph of Stupidity demonstrably contains “the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt” — confirmed in the full essay text ↗, which nowhere contains the phrase “fools and fanatics.”

The citation. Quote Investigator ↗ documents the earliest located printing precisely: “1933 May 10, San Francisco Examiner, Stupidity Rules by Bertrand Russell, Quote Page 10, Column 7, San Francisco, California.” Other references cite the same essay on the same date in the New York American — both were Hearst papers carrying Russell’s syndicated column.

The rewrite, 2001. The “fools and fanatics” version surfaces in InfoWorld in 2001, with an ascription to Russell and an acknowledgement to “A Word a Day.” QI ↗ records no earlier instance and concludes: “Its provenance is uncertain.”

Reference works keep the real wording. Wikiquote’s page for the collection ↗ lists the sentence as “The Triumph of Stupidity,” 10 May 1933 — and the popular “fools and fanatics” sentence appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Bertrand Russell page ↗.
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence in its real setting. Note what surrounds it: this is an argument about political organisation in 1933 Germany, and it ends by admiring people who were sure of themselves.

source.useLine: No rights status can be attached to this wording — its author is unknown. Russell’s actual 1933 sentence is separately in copyright (Bertrand Russell estate; Routledge): a short, credited quote of it is generally fine for talks, teaching, and internal decks; for commercial, published, or large-scale reuse, get permission.
source.rightsNote: The excerpt shown is from an essay first published on 10 May 1933 — after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff — so it remains in copyright, and the Mortals and Others collection that reprints it is a Routledge edition under its own rights. The popular “fools and fanatics” wording is a separate matter: because no one has identified who wrote it or where it first appeared, no rights status can honestly be attached to it, and it certainly cannot be assumed public domain.

author.name: Bertrand Russell
author.kicker: The man who actually had the thought
author.heading: So who was Bertrand Russell?
author.bio: Bertrand Russell was a founder of analytic philosophy and one of the early twentieth century’s most prominent logicians, awarded the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature for writings championing humanitarian ideals and freedom of thought. Alongside the technical work he was a relentless public essayist, and in the early 1930s he wrote a syndicated column for the American press. The 1933 piece that gave rise to this quote was not a detached remark about human psychology — it was written about three months after Hitler took power, and it was about how a civilisation hands itself to its worst elements.

copyAttribution: Bertrand Russell didn't write "The whole problem with the world is that fools are so certain, and wiser people so full of doubts." What he wrote, in "The Triumph of Stupidity" (10 May 1933), was: "The fundamental cause of the trouble is that in the modern world the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt." The popular rewrite has no known source before 2001. — quotle.info

misattribution.heading: How the wording drifted
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this quote from another author — the idea really is Russell’s. What’s wrong is the words, which have been smoothed and shortened on their way around the internet until they no longer match anything he wrote.

items.who: “Fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves”
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ finds this phrasing in the trade publication InfoWorld in 2001, printed “with an ascription to Bertrand Russell and an acknowledgement to ‘A Word a Day’.” QI notes it “differed from Russell’s 1933 statement” and states plainly: “Its provenance is uncertain.”

This shorter form is a truncation of the already-unsourced 2001 variant. Quote Investigator ↗ does not record any version omitting “fanatics,” and no source for it has been found in Russell’s published writing.

Yeats’s 1920 poem “The Second Coming” carries a related thought in entirely his own words: the best lack all conviction while the worst are full of passionate intensity. QI ↗ treats Yeats, Russell and Charles Bukowski as three people who each expressed a related notion distinctly — not as one quote passed between them.

misattribution.truthLine: Russell’s actual sentence, confirmed in the essay text: “The fundamental cause of the trouble is that in the modern world the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt” — The Triumph of Stupidity, 10 May 1933 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Russell wrote this in May 1933, a few months after Hitler became chancellor. It was not a timeless aphorism about clever people and stupid people — it was a political diagnosis of a specific catastrophe. The essay’s argument is that force was falling into the hands of the enemies of civilisation, and that the intelligent had failed to organise against them because they were too busy disagreeing with each other over minor points.

That second half is the part the popular rewrite deletes. Russell was not congratulating doubters. He was complaining about them: the sentence immediately after the famous one says the intelligent “are too individualistic to combine with other intelligent men from whom they differ on minor points.” Doubt, in Russell’s telling, was a political failure — not a badge of wisdom.
detailsBody: A quote about people confidently asserting things they have not checked is itself, almost always, confidently asserted in a form nobody has checked. The version in circulation is a paraphrase of a paraphrase: Russell’s “stupid are cocksure” became “fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves” somewhere before 2001, and that in turn was clipped down to “fools are so certain.”

Russell also went on, in the same paragraph, to praise a group of people who were sure of themselves — the philosophical radicals of a century earlier, who he says “were just as sure of themselves as the Hitlerites are” and who consequently “dominated politics” and advanced the world. Certainty was not his villain. Certainty in the wrong hands was.
context.pull: The rewrite flatters the reader. Russell was accusing him.
